intro.displayText: Sometimes a program meets something it can't handle, like the word two where a number should be. Your mission: keep the Grove potion shop open, even when an order makes no sense!
intro.speechText: Sometimes a program meets something it can't handle, like the word two where a number should be. Your mission is to keep the Grove potion shop open, even when an order makes no sense!

recap.displayText: The shop skips the silly orders and still counts every potion! Your new word is exception: the message C# throws when something goes wrong while a program runs.
recap.speechText: The shop skips the silly orders and still counts every potion! Your new word is exception, which means the message C sharp throws when something goes wrong while a program runs.

intro.displayText: Real programs read files, call services and take user input, and any of those can fail. You'll learn try, catch, finally and exception filters, plus when not to use exceptions at all. Then you'll make an order importer that rejects bad lines with clear messages and keeps going.
intro.speechText: Real programs read files, call services and take user input, and any of those can fail. You'll learn try, catch, finally and exception filters, plus when not to use exceptions at all. Then you'll make an order importer that rejects bad lines with clear messages and keeps going.

recap.displayText: The importer skips bad lines, says exactly what's wrong with each one, and keeps the original exception for whoever has to debug it. The gotcha: only catch what you can handle, because a catch for Exception also hides real bugs, like the null line that still crashes. Next, you'll build families of classes with inheritance.
recap.speechText: The importer skips bad lines, says exactly what's wrong with each one, and keeps the original exception for whoever has to debug it. The gotcha is that you should only catch what you can handle, because a catch for Exception also hides real bugs, like the null line that still crashes. Next, you'll build families of classes with inheritance.

intro.displayText: Every creature in the Grove has a kind and makes a sound. Your mission: add an owl and a snail to the family without writing the same code all over again!
intro.speechText: Every creature in the Grove has a kind and makes a sound. Your mission is to add an owl and a snail to the family without writing the same code all over again!

recap.displayText: The owl hoots, the snail stays quiet, and you only wrote what was different! Your new word is inheritance: one class getting all the code of another.
recap.speechText: The owl hoots, the snail stays quiet, and you only wrote what was different! Your new word is inheritance, which means one class getting all the code of another.

intro.displayText: Real codebases are full of families of types, like payment methods, kinds of user or game units. Inheritance lets them share one base class and replace only what's different. You'll fix a Knight that compiles but ignores its armour, then write a Berserker from scratch.
intro.speechText: Real codebases are full of families of types, like payment methods, kinds of user or game units. Inheritance lets them share one base class and replace only what's different. You'll fix a knight that compiles but ignores its armour, then write a berserker from scratch.

recap.displayText: Your units share one base class, and each changes only what makes it different. The gotcha: a same-named method without override only hides the base one, so code holding a Unit still calls Unit's version, and C# just warns you. Next, interfaces let classes that aren't related make the same promise.
recap.speechText: Your units share one base class, and each changes only what makes it different. The gotcha is that a method with the same name but no override only hides the base one, so code holding a Unit still calls the Unit version, and C sharp just warns you. Next, interfaces let classes that aren't related make the same promise.

intro.displayText: Tonight is the Grove's night parade, and everything that glows gets to light the path. Your mission: help a lantern and a mushroom keep the glowing promise!
intro.speechText: Tonight is the Grove's night parade, and everything that glows gets to light the path. Your mission is to help a lantern and a mushroom keep the glowing promise!

recap.displayText: The path is lit, with a firefly, a lantern and a mushroom glowing side by side! Your new word is interface: a list of jobs that a class promises to do.
recap.speechText: The path is lit, with a firefly, a lantern and a mushroom glowing side by side! Your new word is interface, which means a list of jobs that a class promises to do.

intro.displayText: Most of the time, code shouldn't care which class it's talking to, only that the class can do a job. Interfaces describe that job, and frameworks like ASP.NET Core are built on them. You'll write shipping rates that a checkout compares without knowing what they are, including one rate that wraps any other.
intro.speechText: Most of the time, code shouldn't care which class it's talking to, only that the class can do a job. Interfaces describe that job, and frameworks like A-S-P dot net Core are built on them. You'll write shipping rates that a checkout compares without knowing what they are, including one rate that wraps any other.

recap.displayText: Your checkout compares rates it has never heard of, and FreeOver adds its rule to any of them. The gotcha: every interface member must be public in the class, or it doesn't count, and the class won't compile. Next, records give you data classes that compare by value.

intro.displayText: Grove trading cards are the hottest thing in the forest, and some kids have doubles. Your mission: make a card that knows when it's a copy, then power up a toad!
intro.speechText: Grove trading cards are the hottest thing in the forest, and some kids have doubles. Your mission is to make a card that knows when it's a copy, then power up a toad!

recap.displayText: Your cards print themselves, spot their doubles, and the toad got stronger without changing the original! Your new word is record: a quick way to make a type that just holds data.
recap.speechText: Your cards print themselves, spot their doubles, and the toad got stronger without changing the original! Your new word is record, which means a quick way to make a type that just holds data.

intro.displayText: Most data in real apps is a value: a price, a date range, an address, a song. Records give you value equality, readable output and safe copies in one line, which is why they're everywhere in modern C#. You'll turn a Song class into a record, copy one with with, and fix a playlist whose equality quietly fails.
intro.speechText: Most data in real apps is a value, like a price, a date range, an address or a song. Records give you value equality, readable output and safe copies in one line, which is why they're everywhere in modern C sharp. You'll turn a Song class into a record, copy one with a with expression, and fix a playlist whose equality quietly fails.

recap.displayText: Duplicates disappear, copies leave the original alone, and two playlists with the same songs now count as equal. The gotcha: a record's equality is shallow, so a list inside it is compared by reference unless you write Equals and GetHashCode yourself. Next, LINQ lets you filter, sort and group collections like these.
